title: A Mini North-East in Chennai: The Grocery Stores Keeping Migrant Kitchens Stocked
excerpt: Around 20 northeastern stores line the lanes behind Velachery's Phoenix Mall alone, flying in chayote leaves, napakpi and bamboo shoot for Chennai's eight-state northeastern community.
body:
• A cluster of northeastern grocery stores has grown across Chennai's Besant Nagar, Choolaimedu and Velachery neighbourhoods, serving migrants from all eight northeastern states.
  • Around 20 such stores operate behind Velachery's Phoenix Mall alone — "almost like a mini North-East," says the North East India Welfare Association's Chennai president.
  • The stores fly in produce Chennai markets do not stock: chayote and pumpkin leaves, napakpi herb, bamboo shoot, Sichuan pepper, sticky rice and dried fish.
  • Direct Guwahati flights since 2018 made the trade possible; earlier, one train a week took three days and three nights.

When Kashing Peter from Nagaland opened Northeast Vegetable Store on Chennai's Nelson Manickam Road in 2018, he had two aims: help the northeastern community in Chennai feel closer to home, and open a window for locals into the region's flavours. The tiny store — barely room for two customers inside, the rest spilling onto the road — is now one of dozens across the city, The Hindu reports.

A mini North-East behind the mall

Besant Nagar, Choolaimedu and Velachery have become the popular pockets, drawn by the sizeable northeastern communities living there. "The roads behind Velachery's Phoenix Mall have around 20 northeastern convenience stores. When I walk through these streets, I feel like I am at home because you can meet people from the North-East every few metres. It is almost like a mini North-East," says Wapangtoshi, president of the North East India Welfare Association in Chennai and a resident of the city for 20 years.

"When we migrate to a new place, food is something which must migrate with us."

— Wapangtoshi, president, North East India Welfare Association, Chennai

What the shelves carry that Chennai cannot

The trade exists because the ingredients do not travel through ordinary supply chains. Peter's wife Suiningle Nriame says shoppers come for baby pumpkin, pumpkin leaves and chayote leaves: "While vegetables such as chayote are available in markets across Chennai, their leaves are not sold here, so we import them from parts of the North-East and sell them in our store." At Citywon Mangkung's Awon Northeast shop, produce comes from her home state, Manipur — napakpi, a traditional Manipuri herb, is brought in on request, while mustard leaves are the bestseller, boiled and eaten with pork or cooked into kangsoi with onion, fermented fish, ginger and chilli.

For Maong Nungsang Jamir, owner of the Naga Reju restaurant, the stores rebuilt a ritual that migration had broken. "Back home in Dimapur, we go to the vegetable market, buy produce for the week like bamboo shoot, Sichuan pepper, smoked meat and green veggies, then go to a restaurant for a meal... For years, we were not able to do that when we moved to Chennai, but now it is possible," he says.

Flights made the food possible

The community's Chennai roots go back to the 1980s and 1990s, when northeastern students arrived for engineering degrees and technical training, says Gautam Deori, president of the Assam Association in Chennai; today students from the region are present in large numbers at institutions such as SRM and VIT. The grocery boom, though, waited for logistics. "Earlier, there was only one train a week and it took three days and three nights to reach Chennai. By 2018, the flights began, transport became easier and these stores started coming up," Jamir says.

The exchange now runs both ways. At a Bihu celebration at IIT Madras, Wapangtoshi recalls, people from different cultural backgrounds queued for northeastern food — the same curiosity that brings Chennai locals into the stores for bhut jolokia, sticky rice and fermented bamboo shoot, an acquired taste each community prepares differently. As the Hindu's account ends at Peter's store, where his wife explains a Naga thali to first-time customers: "All you need to be, is curious."
